steps.action:
# The Last Light

Every night, Mara climbed the 127 steps.

She had counted them so many times that she no longer needed to — her legs counted for her, the way lungs count breaths without being asked. On the seventy-third step, there was a slight wobble in the iron railing, a give that felt almost affectionate, like a handshake from an old friend. She always grabbed it anyway.

The lighthouse had been her grandmother's before it was hers. Her grandmother had kept the light burning through three hurricanes, one wedding, and one funeral — her own husband's, when the grief had been so heavy she said she needed somewhere high to put it.

Mara understood that now.

She had come to Pointe Gris two years ago following the end of something she didn't like to name. A job, a person, a version of herself. She had applied for the position almost as a joke, expecting to be laughed at — a woman with soft hands and a graduate degree in architectural history, offering to tend a lighthouse in a county with a population smaller than her old office building.

They had hired her in four days.

The work was simpler than she'd feared and lonelier than she'd expected, which is different from being lonely in the ordinary way. It was a loneliness with texture and purpose. She learned the names of the fishing boats by their running lights — the *Celestine*, the *Agnes B.*, the *Morrow & Sons* — the way you learn the faces of neighbors you've never formally met. She knew when the *Celestine* was running late. She knew when the *Agnes B.* limped in lower than usual, heavy with a good catch.

They didn't know she knew any of this. That felt right somehow.

In October, a storm came that the radio called significant. Mara dragged the backup fuel up the stairs in three trips, her shoulders burning, rain already beginning to slant sideways across the windows. She got the light secured and sat in the watch room with a thermos of coffee and listened to the world come apart outside.

Somewhere in the dark water, she knew, someone was looking for her light.

She thought about that — really thought about it, the way you do when the wind is loud enough to drown your other thoughts. That somewhere out there, in real darkness, a real person was scared, and the single most helpful thing in the world she could do was *shine*. Not fix. Not rescue. Just be a fixed, reliable, visible point that said: *here is where the rocks are. Here is where the safe water is. Here, here, here.*

The storm passed before dawn.

In the morning, the *Celestine* came in, and the *Agnes B.*, and the *Morrow & Sons*, all of them salt-sprayed and slow but upright. Mara watched from the gallery with her coffee going cold in her hands.

She climbed back down the 127 steps.

On the seventy-third, she grabbed the wobbling railing and held on for just a moment longer than she needed to.
